## Clinical Research Trial Overview

Clinical trials may involve novel diagnostic methods or therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, hypo- or hyperthermia, immunotherapy and photodynamic therapy, among others. While most clinical research trials are conducted at colleges of veterinary medicine, a growing number of specialty referral practices are participating in clinical research. For some trials, all visits must occur at the trials institution or practice, but for others there are tests or procedures that could be performed at the general practice.

When discussing the possibility of participating in a clinical trial with pet owners, it is helpful to share that although “experimental,” or “investigational,” the safety and efficacy of new therapies and procedures have often been evaluated first in laboratory animals as well as normal dogs or cats, and the therapy is considered to be of potential benefit to the patient.

Image: Dr. Sarah Sheafor

### Reminder for veterinarians managing pets enrolled in clinical trials

Adherence to the treatment protocol is of vital importance to ensure that the protocol is followed as planned, such that the results are both reliable and meaningful. Any deviation in the pet’s health or management (including medications and supplements) must be reported to the trials institution. For most trials, owners are asked to agree to a necropsy in the event of the death of their pet. Pet owners also may appreciate the translational value of the research in which their pet may be participating. Many naturally-occurring cancers in pet animals closely resemble human cancer and provide meaningful systems for cancer research to benefit both man and animals.

The clinical trials listed on this website are not run under the auspices of the Veterinary Cancer Society. Clinical trials are performed in order to assess the toxicity and/or efficacy of a certain treatment protocol. While the hope is that the investigators will find a less toxic or more effective treatment for cancer, there are no guarantees regarding the outcome of any trials listed on clinical searchable database found on this site.

### Orally administered rapamycin in dogs with cancer

The drug rapamycin is currently approved for immunosuppression during preparatory and maintenance regimens for organ and bone marrow transplant in human patients. Our study evaluates the safety and effectiveness of rapamycin when given orally to dogs with cancer.

### Thermal ablation of cancer in dogs and cats

Our study evaluates the outcome of treating dogs and cats with minimally invasive tumor ablation technologies, including cryoablation and microwave ablation. These methods are used to treat cancers in people, but information in animals is very limited. We previously completed a study on cryoablation in nasal tumor patients; a technique that successfully reduces tumor volume.

### Dogs with glioma or oral melanoma

Glioma is the second-most common type of brain tumor in dogs. Oral melanoma is the most common oral malignancy in dogs and is an extremely malignant tumor with a high degree of local invasiveness and high metastatic propensity. Current treatment options include radiation or chemotherapy and more recently a vaccine; but few dogs are cured and most relapse.

leads.title: UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours

search_hits.retrieved_snippet:
【turn1039news29】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; The University of Queensland (UQ) Gatton has launched a clinical trial testing a new cancer drug, Enzistat, developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune. Led by Professor Rachel Allavena, the trial explores Enzistat’s potential to help dogs with inoperable or terminal tumors. Early data indicate the drug may extend survival and reduce side effects in canine cancer patients. The study is now seeking 60 participating dogs: 30 with inoperable tumours and 30 in palliative care. The goal is to shrink tumors for potential surgery or improve quality of life for terminal cases. Participants must have a cancer diagnosis and veterinary referral, and owners are required to administer the medication twice daily for six weeks and attend three visits to UQ Gatton. While the drug and necessary diagnostics are provided, all other vet costs are the owner’s responsibility. This research also holds promise for human cancer treatments. Interested parties can contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au for more information.
UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

leads.title: Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says

search_hits.retrieved_snippet:
【turn1039news30】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses.

Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients.
Cancer progresses faster in dogs than in people, meaning researchers can receive quicker results with potential treatments in clinical trials with canines. The bone cancer osteosarcoma is more common in dogs than people, so scientists have learned techniques from the animals on how to treat people with the same cancer, and vice versa.
A decade ago, researchers told The Washington Post that dogs were observed more than cats in oncology studies because less was known about feline tumors and cats tended to become more stressed interacting with people.
For their study, van der Weyden and other researchers collected tissue samples from domestic cats from Austria, Canada, England, Germany, New Zealand and Scotland. 
They screened about 1,000 cat genes that are equivalent to human genes associated with cancer. Van der Weyden said she worried they might not find similarities between cat and human cancers, partly because few cat genetic studies had been completed. 
However, in addition to the gene associated with breast cancer in both species, researchers said they found similarities in human and cat cancers affecting their blood, bones, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system.
"I was first of all doing it for the cat," said van der Weyden, senior staff scientist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, a genomics research center in Cambridgeshire, England. "But then to find that there are similarities and we can help humans, that's fantastic."
Researchers found that the chemotherapy drug vincristine was effective against cats' mammary tumors, according to the study, which was published in February. They said that finding could guide veterinary pharmaceutical companies in developing treatment for mammary cancer, which is the third-most-common feline cancer and is typically deadly, according to Cornell University's Feline Health Center.
"Before we just didn't know; we didn't know what drug you could potentially pick," said Wood, who teaches pathology at the University of Guelph in Ontario. "And now there's sort of a list, at least, that could then proceed to clinical trials."
Jaime Modiano, a professor at the University of Minnesota's school of veterinary medicine who was not involved in the research, said the study is a foundation for scientists to learn more about cat and human cancers. However, he said, much more research is required to determine whether the findings can lead to treatments for cats - let alone helping with human cancers.
"It's the first step," Modiano said, "in the journey of a thousand miles."

【turn1039news31】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.1 years ago; A new study, published by researchers from UCSF, UC Davis, and the University of Pittsburgh, presents a groundbreaking cancer treatment for cats that may also benefit human patients with head and neck tumors. The therapy targets STAT3, a transcription factor known to be hyperactivated in about 75% of human tumors. Researchers created a DNA-based decoy molecule that inhibits STAT3 by mimicking the genetic sequences it typically binds to, thereby preventing it from triggering cancer-promoting genes.

In a clinical trial involving 20 pet cats with oral cancer, 35% showed tumor shrinkage or stability, with minimal side effects. One cat, Jak, significantly outlived his prognosis, benefiting from the therapy. The decoy treatment was administered intravenously, an improvement over previous versions requiring direct tumor injection.

The findings revealed immune system changes in treated cats, offering potential biomarkers for identifying patients—both feline and human—who may benefit most. With promising results and improved survival rates in responsive cats, researchers are aiming to fund early-phase human trials while continuing feline studies, suggesting possible future cross-species cancer therapies.
A new cancer treatment for cats could help humans, too
Date: Thu Aug 28 15:00:17 2025 UTC

In a study published Thursday, scientists from UCSF, UC Davis and the University of Pittsburgh describe a promising, first of its kind treatment in pet cats with oral cancer. The authors say the approach could benefit people with head and neck tumors, too.
"There are common features of cancer in cats and cancer in humans," said author Jennifer Grandis, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. "We can learn from each other."
The new treatment targets the STAT3 transcription factor, a protein that binds specific DNA sequences to affect gene expression. "This transcription factor is hyperactivated in almost three-quarters of human tumors," said author Daniel Johnson, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery.
Until now, the protein has proven "incredibly difficult to inhibit," Johnson said. "People have been trying to develop drugs against this protein, STAT3, for many years.

Diagnosed in 2024 with an aggressive mast cell tumor, traditional chemotherapy and surgery failed to stop the cancer. Determined to save her, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AI data processing to analyze Rosie's genomic data, identify cancer mutations, and design a personalized mRNA vaccine with help from experts at the University of NSW.

Developed in collaboration with the UNSW RNA Institute and administered by veterinary researchers at the University of Queensland, the vaccine significantly shrank one of Rosie's large tumors. Mamula, inspired by the loss of his own dog, continues to receive grateful messages from pet owners whose dogs have benefited.
Yale-developed canine cancer vaccine shows promise for dogs, doubling survival rates
Date: Fri Aug  8 09:00:19 2025 UTC

NEW HAVEN - The owner of a 7-year-old golden retriever with an aggressive form of cancer was out of options.
Rick Kneisel, who lives alone in a small city south of Dayton, Ohio, first noticed an issue with his dog, Ranger, in March 2019. A noticeable limp that he initially thought was a pulled muscle turned out to be osteosarcoma, a common and fast-spreading bone cancer in dogs. For Kneisel, 75, the news was "devastating."
Ranger had one of his front legs amputated and endured months of treatment, including chemotherapy and an experimental drug from Ohio State University. But his condition worsened, Kneisel said. The cancer had spread to Ranger's lungs and his chances of survival were dimming.
That's when Kneisel called Dr. Mark Mamula, an immunologist and professor at the Yale School of Medicine, who, along with a team of researchers, were developing a canine cancer vaccine that's now changing the outlook for dogs with cancer and offering hope to their owners.
"You start doing the numbers with 90 million dogs, there are large populations of dogs in this country that are destined to get cancers," Mamula said
Mamula's quest for a canine cancer treatment was motivated by a personal loss. About a dozen years ago, his 10-year-old golden retriever, Savannah, died of hemangiosarcoma, an aggressive form of cancer in dogs that arises from blood vessels, according to PetMD. 
"I realized at the time that the tools the veterinarian oncologists have at their disposal were just not what one can find in treating human cancers by comparison," he said.
In search of a solution, he teamed up with Gerald Post, then a Norwalk-based veterinarian oncologist, in 2015. Together, the two launched an early-phase study for a novel cancer vaccine - work that Mamula said "paved the way" for the clinical trials now underway, although Post is no longer involved in the research.
Since the initial study, Mamula and his team have gained a better understanding of which dog breeds and cancer types the vaccine might treat most effectively, allowing them to refine their approach.
Mamula called his cancer vaccine research "the most satisfying work that I've done" in his more than 35 years at Yale. He often gets emails from dog owners a year or two - sometimes even three - after their pets receive immunotherapy, sharing updates on their post-cancer lives.
But the messages that resonate most, he said, come from older, usually widowed owners whose dogs are beloved companions or service animals. They write to say they're "still a happy family" with a long-term survivor.
"I sleep well at night getting those types of emails," Mamula said.
Dog owners should contact vet clinics directly to enroll in the clinical trials. A list of locations is available on the websites for TheraJan and the Canine Cancer Alliance.

leads.title: Cats give genetic clues to better cancer treatments

search_hits.retrieved_snippet:
【turn1039news34】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute has revealed that domestic cats share significant genetic similarities with humans in the development of cancer, offering new avenues for treatment in both species. Researchers analyzed 13 types of feline tumors from nearly 500 cats across five countries by sequencing DNA from cancerous and healthy tissues. They found mutations in about 1,000 genes linked to human cancers, across various tumor types like blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system cancers.

One key finding relates to feline breast cancer, where over half showed mutations in the FBXW7 gene—rare in humans but linked to worse outcomes. Tests with common chemotherapy drugs such as vincristine and vinorelbine successfully suppressed tumor growth in cat tissues with FBXW7 mutations. This discovery positions felines as potential early test subjects for treatments, especially where human clinical trials are harder to implement.

The research highlights the value of "comparative oncology," studying cancer across species, akin to research on elephants' resistance to tumors. Experts suggest these cross-species studies could offer vital insights into cancer prevention and treatment for humans.

Cats give genetic clues to better cancer treatments 
Date: Thu Feb 19 19:00:08 2026 UTC

Domestic cats have emerged as unlikely allies in the fight against human cancers, after scientists found close similarities between genetic changes that drive the deadly disease in both species.
The discoveries from the first large-scale DNA study of feline tumours open up new ideas for treatments for people and pets, researchers from the UK's Wellcome Sanger Institute said.  
Scientists are increasingly focusing on genetic lessons from animals that are prone to cancers or unusually resilient to them. Household species are of particular interest because they are exposed to some of the same environmental risks as their human companions.  
"By comparing cancer genomics across different species, we gain a greater understanding of what causes the disease," said Bailey Francis, a Wellcome Sanger researcher and co-first author of a paper published in the journal Science on Thursday. "This could help experts in the veterinary field as well as those studying cancer in humans."
The Wellcome Sanger researchers and colleagues from countries including Canada and Switzerland examined 13 cat cancer types using tissue samples collected by vets from almost 500 domestic animals across five countries. They sequenced DNA from tumours and healthy tissues to look for about 1,000 genes that are associated with cancer in people. The felines showed similar genetic mutations to humans in cases of blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal and central nervous system tumours.
One of the most intriguing findings was for cat breast cancers, more than half of which showed a mutation in a gene called FBXW7. The change is far rarer in human mammary cancers, but the prognosis for the sufferer is worse when it is present.
The researchers found that the chemotherapeutic drugs vincristine and vinorelbine, used to treat diseases such as leukaemia, curbed the growth of the FBXW7-mutated tumours in cat tissues. 
This suggested an initial test of the drugs' effectiveness against breast cancer could be done in felines, as a trial in people would be hard to organise because of the FBXW7 mutation's relative scarcity.

Tout au long de l'année, des essais cliniques sont mis en œuvre afin d'améliorer la prise en charge des animaux de compagnie. L'EnvA, dans ses cliniques, propose aux propriétaires d'en bénéficier en participant à des études.
Ophtalmologie

Une étude clinique pour un nouveau traitement médical de la cataracte diabétique chez le chien menée à l'hôpital des animaux de compagnie.

 

Une étude est en cours à l'école nationale vétérinaire d'Alfort afin d’optimiser la prise en charge des entéropathies exsudatives, maladie complexe dont le pronostic peut être sombre. Les spécialistes de l'hôpital des animaux de compagnie recrutent des chiens avec entéropathies exsudatives dans le cadre d'une étude afin de mieux comprendre cette affection.

La prise en charge des chiens a donc pour objectif d’améliorer le pronostic en proposant une alimentation ciblée et un suivi régulier.
L'EnvA recrute ainsi tout chien présentant une hypo-albuminémie et/ou des troubles digestifs.

L'étude n'entraine aucun risque supplémentaire pour l'animal et permet un suivi gratuit durant plusieurs semaines.

Table des matières

 Pour toute question :

## Besoin d’aide dans vos recherches?

Trouver un essai clinique peut être une démarche difficile et complexe. C’est pour cela que notre partenaire Q-CROC a mis en place Onco+, un service d’accompagnement gratuit, offert pour toute personne à la recherche d’un essai clinique en oncologie au Québec.

Ce service est offert en collaboration avec la Fondation québécoise du cancer. Une infirmière spécialisée en oncologie de notre Ligne Info-cancer vous aidera personnellement tout au long du processus de recherche d’un essai clinique. Nous assurerons la confidentialité et la sécurité de vos informations.

Contactez-nous par téléphone au 1 877 336-4443, poste 115 ou en remplissant ce formulaire en ligne pour obtenir de l’assistance dans vos recherches. 

 

Image: Onco+2023

  * Vous venez d’être diagnostiqué à un stade avancé de cancer
  * Vous avez un cancer et ne répondez plus aux traitements disponibles
  * Vous êtes en rémission, mais êtes à risque de voir votre cancer récidiver
  * Votre cancer pourrait se propager à d’autres parties de votre corps
  * Vous venez d’être diagnostiqué d’un cancer rare, agressif ou difficile à traiter

 

## Vous aimeriez participer à un essai clinique?

Découvrez la recherche clinique au Québec et le témoignage d’un patient qui partage son parcours et son expérience en tant que participant à un essai clinique.   

Si vous désirez en apprendre davantage sur les essais cliniques en oncologie au Québec et évaluer si la participation à un essai clinique pourrait être une option pour vous, veuillez consulter le site de notre partenaire Q-CROC.

 

Image: Q-CROC

Dogs and cats develop naturally occurring tumors that closely resemble human malignancies in histopathology, molecular alterations, tumor microenvironments, and treatment response. These species also share exposure to environmental carcinogens and demonstrate conserved pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) profiles of several chemotherapeutic agents. Comme les humains, les chiens et les chats peuvent développer des cancers ou des tumeurs dans différentes parties de leur corps. Ces dernières années, l’oncologie vétérinaire a connu des avancées rapides. L’augmentation du nombre de cas permet de renforcer notre expérience et notre expertise, et de proposer des techniques de diagnostic et des traitements toujours plus performants (imagerie, analyses de laboratoire, radiothérapie, etc.).

Chez les animaux, les effets secondaires sont généralement moins fréquents et moins marqués que chez l’Homme. Ils peuvent toutefois apparaître et se traduire par une perte d’appétit, des nausées, des vomissements ou de la fatigue. Des traitements adaptés peuvent être mis en place afin de limiter ces effets tout en restant compatibles avec la chimiothérapie.

La radiothérapie

Chez certains chiens, des rougeurs cutanées peuvent également survenir, entraînant parfois des démangeaisons et du léchage.

Chez les chats, des desquamations peuvent être observées, la peau ayant tendance à s’écailler.

Ces effets secondaires restent généralement modérés et bien pris en charge.

## Quelle est la fréquence du cancer chez les chiens et les chats ?

Bien que n’importe quel chat ou chien puisse avoir le cancer, il est plus fréquent chez les animaux plus âgés. Selon l’American Veterinary Medical Association, les chiens ont à peu près autant de risques que les humains en ce qui concerne le cancer, avec près de la moitié de les chiens gériatriques (ceux de plus de 10 ans) développent un cancer à un moment donné.

## Clinical Trials Now Enrolling

#### CALL FOR PATIENTS: Clinical Trial for Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Dogs

Study Title: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients

Eligibility: Any dog weighing 5kg or above with at least one cutaneous soft tissue sarcoma lesion that is greater than 1.7cm in diameter is eligible to enroll. All dogs that meet the study criteria will receive the study drug (no placebo) followed by surgical removal of the tumor 1 week later.

Study Purpose: This clinical trial evaluates the safety, feasibility, and biological effects of a newly designed immunotherapy. Specifically, the study is evaluating the injection of investigational T-cell engagers (TCEs) directly into tumors (intratumorally) in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS). TCEs are engineered antibodies that physically connect T cells to cancer cells by targeting specific markers (CD3 or CD28 on T cells, and B7-H3 or PD-L1 on cancer cells), triggering the immune system to destroy tumor cells.

Similar therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells (e.g. leukemia), however, they have had more limited success in solid tumors. This is in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing side effects. Delivering this dual-TCE combination directly into the tumor aims to achieve localized anti-cancer activity at lower individual doses, reducing the potential for severe whole-body side effects.

#### Treatment Objectives

The clinical trial is designed to test varying TCE doses and formulations. A fluorescent tracking dye is mixed into the injection to trace placement and to aid in assessing the anti-tumor response to the therapy. Following TCE injection, as part of the standard care plan for dogs with STS, surgery is then performed to remove the tumor at VRCCO.  Researchers will analyze the removed tissue via histopathology to evaluate immune cell activation, T-cell accumulation, and tumor cell death.

#### Safety Measures, Risks, and Potential Benefits

While procedures like blood draws, ultrasound, anesthesia, and surgery carry standard medical risks, the investigational TCEs also carry the potential risks of temporary discomfort, minor bleeding, redness, and irritation at the injection site. Although this study seeks to reduce these risks through careful selection of the TCEs and the intratumoral doses to be used, these and other side effects could occur including overactive immune responses/allergic reactions, gastro-intestinal upset, and other potential unforeseen adverse reactions. How cats may prove an unexpected ally in fight against cancer
Date: Thu Feb 19 18:59:53 2026 UTC

A scientific study of hundreds of pet cats suggests that an unexpected ally in the fight against cancer may be curled up on the sofa.
Some cancers are frustratingly hard to study in people because they are rare. In cats, however, comparable tumours can be far more common. 
The research shows that many of these feline cancers are driven by the same genetic mutations as their human counterparts.
According to the scientists, studying the common animal versions of rare human diseases may reveal patterns and insights that would otherwise remain hidden.
One of the most promising areas is in the treatment of mammary tumours, which in cats are often incredibly aggressive and mirror some of the toughest-to-treat forms of human breast cancer.
The researchers found that many feline mammary tumours carry the same "faulty" genetic switches seen in women. That raises the possibility that drugs already used or being tested for human patients could be repurposed for cats. In turn, careful observation of how cats respond to them might help refine treatment strategies in people.
• Rhys Blakely: Monkeys or microchips? The debate over animal testing won't die
The study, published in the journal Science, is part of a broader approach known as "One Medicine", which is based on the idea that veterinary and human medicine should inform one another.
An international team led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute in Britain, the Ontario Veterinary College and the University of Bern analysed tumours from 493 pet cats across five countries, spanning 13 cancer types.
They examined the feline versions of roughly 1,000 genes known to be involved in human cancers, comparing DNA from each tumour with healthy tissue from the same animal. The result is the first comprehensive genetic map - or "oncogenome" - of cancer in domestic cats.
"The genetics of domestic cat tumours are no longer a 'black box'," said Louise van der Weyden of the Wellcome Sanger Institute, co-senior author of the study.

【turn1042news29】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.1 years ago; US-Forscher haben in einer in „Cancer Cell“ veröffentlichten Studie eine neue Therapie gegen Plattenepithelkarzinome im Kopf- und Halsbereich (HNSCC) getestet – erstmals an Hauskatzen. Diese Krebsform gilt beim Menschen wie bei Tieren als besonders aggressiv und schwer behandelbar. Das getestete Medikament zielt auf den Transkriptionsfaktor STAT3, der das Tumorwachstum fördert. Bei 35 % der 20 teilnehmenden Katzen zeigte sich ein positives Ansprechen auf die Therapie mit minimalen Nebenwirkungen. Die Behandlung führte zu teilweiser Besserung oder stabiler Erkrankung, mit einer durchschnittlichen Überlebenszeit von 161 Tagen bei betroffenen Katzen.

Die Studie unterstreicht das Potenzial, klinische Studien an Haustieren durchzuführen, da deren Tumore ähnliche Eigenschaften wie menschliche Tumore aufweisen. Zusätzlich konnte eine verstärkte Immunantwort durch erhöhtes PD-1 beobachtet werden, was Ansatzpunkte für eine Kombination mit Checkpoint-Inhibitoren bietet. Der Ansatz zeigt, dass Haustiere vielversprechendere Modelle als Labormäuse sein könnten. Die Studienautoren planen bereits weitere klinische Tests – sowohl für Tiere als auch für Menschen. Die Forschung eröffnet damit neue Wege für eine effektivere und gleichzeitig tierfreundlichere Krebstherapie.
Katzen, die in der Krebsforschung oft wenig Beachtung finden, könnten davon stark profitieren. Die Idee, das HNSCC-Medikament an Hauskatzen zu testen, kam der Erstautorin Jennifer Grandis in einem Gespräch mit ihrer Schwester, einer Tierärztin. „Es gibt eine bemerkenswerte klinische, histopathologische und immunologische Ähnlichkeit zwischen HNSCC bei Katzen und Menschen", berichtet die Krebsmedizinerin jetzt mit ihren Kollegen in „Cell Cancer".  Zu den Katzen, die von der ersten klinischen Studie profitierten, zählte ein neunjähriger schwarzer Kater namens Jakiro, oder einfach „Jak". Als bei ihm ein HNSCC diagnostiziert wurde, erklärte der Tierarzt seinen Haltern, ihr Liebling hätte nur noch sechs bis acht Wochen zu leben. Es sei wie ein Schlag in die Magengrube gewesen, erinnert sich Tina Thomas, die Besitzerin. „Wir wollten mehr Zeit mit ihm verbringen. Als ich von dieser klinischen Studie erfuhr, wusste ich, dass ich ihn daran teilhaben lassen wollte." Mehrere Monate statt nur Wochen Jak wurde einen Monat lang wöchentlich behandelt; sechs Dosen waren es insgesamt, die man allen vierbeinigen Probanden intravenös spritzte.

Faculdade de Medicina Veterinária e Zootecnia da USP

Cães com câncer na região anal podem ajudar na busca do câncer em animais e humanos

Se você possui um cão com câncer anal e que ainda não recebeu nenhum tratamento, ele pode ajudar a Faculdade de Medicina Veterinária e Zootecnia (FMVZ) da USP na investigação sobre cura de câncer em animais e humanos. A pesquisa, que é conduzida pela doutoranda Karina D’Angelo Campos, tem como orientadora a professora Denise Tabacchi Fantoni e está sendo desenvolvida no Departamento de Cirurgia (VCI).

O objetivo do estudo é  avaliar tumores perianais em cães e os efeitos de diferentes medicamentos anestésicos e analgésicos sobre a recuperação pós-cirúrgica e o sistema imunológico, além de investigar se existe correlação entre esses aspectos e o prognóstico da doença.

Podem participar cães de todas raças, gêneros e idades, desde que apresentem câncer suspeito ou confirmado na região anal (nódulo ou massa próximo ao ânus) e que ainda não tenham recebido tratamento. Devem ter comportamento dócil, ou não muito agressivo, e não estejam acometidos de doenças crônicas avançadas como doença cardíaca ou renal, entre outras.

Os proprietários que quiserem incluir seus animais na pesquisa devem entrar em contato com a pesquisadora pelo número (11) 960320242, até o dia 15 de maio, para obter mais informações para avaliação.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada. By making this information easier to access, the registry supports continued research and progress in veterinary medicine and canine health care.

If you are interested in a clinical trial for your dog, begin by discussing the study and your dog’s potential eligibility with your veterinary care provider.

 

AVMA Clinical Trials

#### National Cancer Institute, Comparative Oncology Program

The Comparative Oncology Program develops and conducts clinical trials in partnership with veterinary teaching institutions throughout the United States. Dogs enrolled in these studies receive care from board-certified veterinary oncologists committed to improving comfort, quality of life, and cancer care for companion animals.

The knowledge gained through this research may help advance the understanding of cancer and support future progress in both canine and human oncology.

National Cancer Institute

#### PetCure Oncology

PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.

PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

PetCure Oncology Clinical Trials

#### ACI Biosciences

Network conducting trials at participating private practices.

ACI Biosciences Clinical Trials

### Specialty and Referral Practices

## Canada

## Keep in Mind

Clinical trials may explore new approaches to diagnosing or supporting dogs with cancer. These may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, temperature-based therapies, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and other emerging approaches.

Although many clinical trials take place at veterinary colleges and teaching hospitals, a growing number of specialty and referral practices also participate in canine cancer research. Some studies require every appointment to be completed at the participating institution, while others may allow certain tests, procedures, or follow-up visits to be handled by a dog’s regular veterinary team.

The words “experimental” and “investigational” can understandably feel concerning. Before a new therapy or procedure reaches a veterinary clinical trial, researchers have typically completed earlier stages of evaluation. However, unknowns may remain regarding its safety, effectiveness, or potential side effects. A study is offered because researchers believe the approach may provide meaningful benefits, but participation does not guarantee a positive outcome.

Pet parents should review the study’s purpose, requirements, possible benefits, known and unknown risks, costs, and available alternatives with the clinical trial team and their dog’s veterinary care provider before making a decision.

# ReachGlio: nuevo ensayo clínico para perros con glioma de alto grado

17 septiembre, 2026 Hospital Veterinario Puchol Neurologia

El Hospital Veterinario Puchol ha iniciado el reclutamiento de pacientes para ReachGlio, un Ensayo Clínico Veterinario dirigido a perros con diagnóstico presuntivo de glioma de alto grado, uno de los tumores cerebrales más complejos en neurología y oncología veterinaria.

El estudio ha sido autorizado por laAgencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios (AEMPS)y está financiado en el marco de la convocatoria europea TRANSCAN-3, orientada a impulsar la investigación traslacional en cáncer.

El Ensayo Clínico Veterinario se desarrollará en elHospital Veterinario Puchol, en el marco de un proyecto de investigación promovido por la Unidad de Neurooncología del Instituto de Salud Carlos III, y coordinado por la Universidad Camilo José Cela.

Más allá de evaluar una nueva estrategia terapéutica en el contexto de un ensayo clínico, ReachGlio busca responder a una pregunta especialmente relevante en neurooncología:

¿Podemos conseguir que los tratamientos antitumorales lleguen de forma más eficaz a las células tumoradas en el cerebro?

## Glioma en perros: uno de los grandes retos de la neurología veterinaria

Los gliomas son tumores primarios del sistema nervioso central que se originan a partir de células de estirpe glial. Dentro de este grupo se incluyen fundamentalmente a los oligodendrogliomas y los astrocitomas.

Aparecen principalmente en perros adultos o geriátricos y se ha descrito una mayor predisposición en determinadas razas, especialmente entre las braquicéfalas.

Si nos preguntamos cuales son los síntomas de un tumor cerebral en un perro, estos dependen de la localización y extensión del tumor. Entre las manifestaciones que pueden aparecer se encuentran:

  * crisis epilépticas de nueva aparición;
  * cambios de comportamiento;
  * alteraciones del nivel de consciencia;
  * desorientación;
  * alteraciones de la marcha;
  * déficits neurológicos focales.
ImageGlioma presente en perros y humanos

Esa protección, imprescindible para el funcionamiento normal del cerebro, supone también un desafío terapéutico: algunos medicamentos pueden tener dificultades para alcanzar concentraciones terapéuticas en los tumores cerebrales o gliomas caninos.

Además, ésta barrera hematoencefálica no es uniforme en todo el tumor, algunas zonas pueden ser más permeables, mientras que otras continúan limitando significativamente la entrada de determinados tratamientos.

Por tanto, conseguir que un fármaco llegue al cerebro no significa necesariamente que alcance de manera suficiente todas las áreas relevantes del tumor.

Este es precisamente uno de los retos que investiga ReachGlio.

## ¿Qué estudia exactamente ReachGlio?

El Ensayo Clínico Veterinario evaluará una estrategia basada en la administración deSNGR-TNF en combinación con temozolomida.

Según el protocolo del estudio, SNGR-TNF es un agente dirigido a la vasculatura tumoral cuya finalidad es inducir una modificación transitoria y controlada de la barrera hematoencefálica.

El objetivo es estudiar si esta modificación puede favorecer una mayor penetración de la temozolomida, el principal quimioterápico utilizado para el tratamiento de glioma canino y humano de alto grado.

Por tanto, ReachGlio no evalúa únicamente un nuevo esquema de tratamiento. Su planteamiento científico consiste en estudiar si es posiblemodificar temporalmente las condiciones de acceso al tumor para favorecer la exposición al fármaco.

Se trata de un ensayo piloto de naturaleza exploratoria, por lo que uno de sus principales objetivos será obtener información sobre farmacodinamia, tolerabilidad y seguridad que permita orientar futuras fases de investigación.

## Un diseño con ajuste dinámico de dosis

Otro de los aspectos relevantes del estudio es su diseño.

ReachGlio utilizará un modelo secuencial con ajuste dinámico de dosis, en el que las decisiones se tomarán teniendo en cuenta parámetros de seguridad y biomarcadores farmacodinámicos.

Este planteamiento permite incorporar la información obtenida progresivamente durante el ensayo y ajustar la dosis de acuerdo con los criterios de seguridad y los datos farmacodinámicos establecidos en el protocolo.

La autorización de la AEMPS implica además que el estudio debe desarrollarse bajo un protocolo previamente definido, con requisitos específicos de seguridad, seguimiento, documentación y bienestar animal.

## ¿Qué perros pueden ser candidatos?

ReachGlio está dirigido aperros con diagnóstico presuntivo de glioma de alto grado y un peso corporal igual o superior a 7 kg, que además cumplan los criterios establecidos en el protocolo del estudio.

La identificación de un posible candidato comienza mucho antes de la inclusión en el estudio.

El papel del veterinario generalista y del veterinario remitente resulta especialmente importante ante pacientes que presentan signos compatibles con enfermedad prosencefálica, especialmente:

  * crisis epilépticas de nueva aparición en un perro adulto
  * cambios conductuales
  * alteración del estado mental
  * déficits neurológicos focales

Tras la evaluación neurológica y las pruebas de diagnóstico por imagen correspondientes, los pacientes que presenten hallazgos compatibles con los criterios iniciales podrán ser valorados individualmente para estudiar su posible inclusión en el estudio.

## ¿Qué implica participar en ReachGlio?

Los perros incluidos recibirán seis ciclos de tratamiento, con un intervalo de 21 días entre cada ciclo.

El protocolo contempla visitas al Hospital Veterinario Puchol para la administración intravenosa del tratamiento y su monitorización, junto con medicación oral en domicilio.

El seguimiento incluirá:

  * evaluaciones neurológicas periódicas;
  * controles analíticos;
  * resonancias magnéticas con contraste para valoración de los cambios en el tumor;
  * monitorización de posibles efectos adversos;
  * y valoración de la evolución de la lesión.

El protocolo contempla también la confirmación histopatológica post mortem del tumor, realizada por laboratorios especializados.

ImageGlioma cerebral observado en necropsia.

Aunque este aspecto requiere una comunicación especialmente sensible con las familias, permite obtener información muy valiosa para la investigación, ya que hace posible relacionar los hallazgos de la resonancia magnética y la evolución clínica con las características histológicas del tumor. Esta información es imprescindible para comprender mejor la enfermedad y, particularmente, para interpretar los resultados obtenidos durante el ensayo.

## El Hospital Veterinario Puchol desarrollará la fase clínica veterinaria

La incorporación del Hospital Veterinario Puchol al proyecto permitirá trasladar esta investigación al contexto clínico, trabajando con pacientes caninos con tumores que aparecen de forma espontánea, dentro de un entorno clínico especializado y bajo un protocolo específicamente autorizado.

El hospital será el centro encargado de desarrollar el ensayo clínico, con participación de su Servicio de Neurología y de los recursos necesarios para la evaluación clínica, el diagnóstico por imagen, la administración del tratamiento y el seguimiento de los pacientes.

Los procedimientos específicamente contemplados dentro del protocolo de investigación, incluyendo el tratamiento, las resonancias de seguimiento y las analíticas vinculadas al estudio, están financiados en el marco de TRANSCAN-3 y no supondrán un coste adicional para los propietarios.

Sin embargo, el principal valor de este proyecto no es económico.

ReachGlio representa la posibilidad de que determinados pacientes con una enfermedad neurológica grave accedan a una estrategia terapéutica experimental única dentro de un Ensayo Clínico regulado, protocolizado y estrechamente monitorizado, pudiéndose beneficiar de las nuevas oportunidades terapéuticas que ofrecen moléculas actualmente en desarrollo

Y representa también algo esencial para el futuro de la medicina veterinaria: seguir generando evidencia allí donde todavía existen preguntas sin respuesta.

### Información para veterinarios

El reclutamiento de pacientes comenzó el 1 de septiembre de 2026.

Los veterinarios que atiendan a un perro con una lesión intracraneal compatible con un glioma de alto grado pueden contactar con el Hospital Veterinario Puchol para valorar conjuntamente si el paciente cumple inicialmente los criterios necesarios para ser considerado candidato al ensayo.

La puesta en marcha de ReachGlio supone un nuevo paso en el compromiso del Hospital Veterinario Puchol con una medicina basada en la especialización, el rigor científico, la innovación y la investigación clínica, especialmente en enfermedades complejas en las que todavía es necesario seguir avanzando.

# About the Comparative Oncology Program

The Comparative Oncology Program (COP) conducts research to better understand the biology of cancer and improve the assessment of novel treatments for humans by treating pet dogs with naturally occurring cancer. These patients receive cutting-edge care and access to clinical trials that evaluate new treatment options for cancer. Results from these studies support further development of human clinical trials and are leading the way in the fight against cancer in humans and their pets.

The COP designs and conducts clinical trials in collaboration with academic veterinary institutions across the United States. Centrally managed by COP, this network is called the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium (COTC). Pet animals with naturally occurring cancers that are enrolled in COTC studies are treated by board-certified veterinary oncologists who share our goal of alleviating the suffering of companion animals with cancer. 

Through these trials, COP and COTC researchers gather crucial information on treatment response, toxicity, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, dose, regimen, schedule, biomarkers of response and responding histologies that applies to and will benefit both animals and humans with cancers.

Your Dog Is a Secret Weapon in the Fight Against Cancer
Date: Thu May 11 17:01:09 2023 UTC

Jellybean continues to defy expectations. The 5-year-old Labrador retriever mix jumps up and down from her favorite spot on the couch and walks around the living room with such ease, it's as if she hadn't ever had metastatic cancer. Her owners, Patricia and Zach Mendonca, still can't quite believe the miracle. "She's got a little bit more of a tug to her step," Patricia says.
Jellybean was diagnosed with bone cancer in her hind leg almost three years ago. Despite amputation and chemotherapy, the cancerous cells quickly spread through her blood to her lungs, as they do in 90 percent of cases in dogs. Survival time at this stage averages two months. "We didn't have any hopes of curing her," says Patricia. "We were pretty devastated."
So in November 2020, the Mendoncas enrolled Jellybean in a clinical trial at Tufts University, about an hour's drive from their home in Rhode Island in the US. Jellybean was given a trio of pills, at no cost, which the Mendoncas stuffed daily into her favorite chicken-flavored treats. By Christmas, Jellybean's tumors had begun to shrink, and they haven't come back since. The response surprised even the vets treating Jellybean, and raised hopes that these drugs could help not just other dogs, but humans too.
Jellybean's bone cancer, osteosarcoma, also affects people-particularly children and teens. Fortunately, it's relatively rare: Some 26,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year. The problem is that there haven't been any new treatments for over 35 years, says veterinary oncologist Amy LeBlanc, and those available aren't very effective. Osteosarcoma patients have a survival rate of only around 30 percent if cancerous cells spread to other parts of the body.
Canine studies, like Jellybean's trial, could change all this. Cancers that arise in pet dogs are molecularly and microscopically similar to cancers in people-in the case of osteosarcoma, the similarities are striking. When compared under the microscope, a canine tissue sample and a human tissue sample of a tumor are indistinguishable. But while it's thankfully rare in humans, osteosarcoma is at least 10 times as common in dogs-meaning there are huge numbers of canine cancer patients out there to help with research and drug testing. "The families and dogs that participate are an important piece of the puzzle in moving this research forward," says Cheryl London, the veterinary oncologist at Tufts University's Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine who is treating Jellybean.
Importantly, dogs are not subject to the same federal regulations that limit treatment options for humans; veterinarians are much freer to use existing drugs off-label against diseases for which there aren't currently good treatments. All told, this makes for quicker and cheaper clinical trials.
Such trials are part of the Cancer Moonshot initiative that US president Joe Biden relaunched last year and for which he has asked Congress to provide an additional $2.8 billion in the 2024 budget. "They're designed to fill a knowledge gap that is not sufficiently filled by traditional studies in mice or by data that cannot yet be easily gathered in humans," says LeBlanc, who directs the Comparative Oncology Program at the US National Cancer Institute. The program oversees clinical trials on dogs with cancer, which are carried out by Tufts and 21 other veterinary universities in the US and Canada.
Apart from the fact that many dogs get cancer and are treated every year, they are also better suited for studies than laboratory mice. Tumors occur naturally in dogs and they are exposed to a similar living environment as humans; in comparison, researchers raise and keep mice in cages, and study the spread and treatment of cancer under artificial conditions, by injecting the mice with malignant cells. In addition, the accelerated lifespan of dogs can help researchers see results quicker than they might in a human study.
Dogs also respond to treatments in similar ways to humans, as several clinical studies in recent years have shown. In 2019, scientists at Colorado State University completed a trial of 28 dogs with osteosarcoma that had spread to the lungs. In addition to a commercially available cancer drug, they prescribed the dogs a common blood pressure drug, losartan, which acts on the immune system by blocking the recruitment of a type of white blood cell that stimulates tumor growth. Three years later, the scientists reported that this pair of drugs had helped shrink or stabilize lung tumors in 50 percent of the dogs. (Jellybean is receiving these along with a third drug, not yet approved for humans, as part of a parallel study at Tufts University.)
Already this losartan research is having a knock-on effect for humans. Around 40 children with resistant or recurrent osteosarcoma are now receiving losartan and the human equivalent of the canine cancer drug to determine the safety and dose range of the treatment. It's a promising step, but according to Steve Dow, veterinarian and director of the Center for Immune and Regenerative Medicine at Colorado State University, it's too early to make an assessment of the impact it could have in people, because the human trial "is not at the high-dose range yet, which is where we saw activity in dogs."
But another clinical trial, involving an experimental vaccine, is already a step further: Scientists and doctors are testing how effective the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes is at treating human osteosarcoma patients. This nasty bacterium usually causes food poisoning, but in its weakened form, it stimulates the immune system. In dogs, immune cells have been shown to patrol the body after vaccination and destroy any cancer cells remaining after conventional therapy. The study to see whether the same happens in humans is due to be completed later this year.

LeBlanc is excited about the results of these trials. But, she says, the canine work the National Cancer Institute oversees is also helping scientists better understand cancer in general. Blood tests and subsequent DNA analyses, for example, provide important insights into the genes that drive the development and growth of cancers. "We are poised to release a significant amount of data this year and show what we can learn about dogs with osteosarcoma-where they share key similarities, but also where they're different," she says.
Medical companies have also recognized the potential of pet cancer data, especially in the field of precision medicine, where patients receive personalized treatments that target cancer-causing mutations that are specific to their genes. This personalized approach is considered the holy grail of cancer therapy-but it relies on analyzing huge amounts of genetic information. Gaining enough data to reliably predict how a drug will perform is one of the biggest challenges when it comes to developing a new cancer treatment, says James Zou, an assistant professor of biomedical data science at Stanford University.
In a study published in January this year, Zou and his colleagues, working with One Health Company, which focuses on precision medicine, showed that dogs can expand the pool of useful clinical data. With the help of a computer model, the team compared the genetic mutations and treatment outcomes of dogs with cancer. They drew on a dataset of nearly 800 dogs treated for different types of cancer in American veterinary clinics and whose tumor tissue had been sequenced to detect mutations. Based on a comparison with data from a small number of human studies, the team found that dogs and humans who have similar genetic mutations and receive similar treatments have similar clinical outcomes-thus showing that dog data can help with developing human drugs.
Once researchers have access to a canine dataset like this, and have analyzed which gene-drug combinations appear to be effective in dogs, existing drugs could then be repurposed or further developed for human use without having to start from scratch. The traditional pipeline of a single cancer drug is at least 10 years and costs billions of dollars, in part because recruiting enough people for clinical trials is so difficult, time-consuming, and costly. Applying machine learning to dog cancer data could speed up the process.
This will be needed if President Biden's overall cancer vision is to be met. He wants to reduce cancer-related mortality rates by at least 50 percent over the next 25 years. This will require progress not only on the deadliest but also the rarest human cancers, including those of the bones, lymph glands, and brain, where clinical expertise is still lacking and pharmaceutical companies have had less incentive to conduct trials because the potential market is small. Anything that can bring down the costs of drug testing for these conditions will be massively helpful.
LeBlanc believes Zou's research underscores the promise of precision medicine, and sets the stage for follow-up studies in which drugs are prescribed to dogs in a controlled setting and data is gathered over a period of time. But she would like to see research and drug development continue to be guided by the principle that dogs with cancer are not just study subjects, but first and foremost patients themselves. "Their care and welfare as they help us along this journey are always going to be our top priority," she says.
This is also the top priority for Jellybean's owners. She is the only one of the 23 dogs who is still alive after receiving the same treatment as part of the Tufts University trial. The median survival time was about five months. "The work that Tufts has done and the science behind it have touched our lives so strongly and saved our dog," says Patricia. She is glad to know that the ongoing treatment and regular check-ups could help other dogs and people in the future. "But on a day-to-day basis, it's just the fact that she's still with us."

Objectives: Lung cancer remains a significant global public health challenge and is still one of the leading cause of cancer-related death in Argentina. This study aims to assess the disease and economic burden of lung cancer in the country. Study design: Burden of disease study Methods. A mathematical model was developed to estimate the disease burden and direct medical cost attributable to lung cancer. Epidemiological parameters were obtained from local statistics, the Global Cancer Observatory, the Global Burden of Disease databases, and a literature review. Direct medical costs were estimated through micro-costing. Costs were expressed in US dollars (US$), April 2023 (1 US$ =216.38 argentine pesos). A second-order Monte Carlo simulation was performed to estimate the uncertainty. Results: Considering approximately 10,000 deaths, 12,000 incident cases, and 14,000 5-year prevalent cases, the economic burden of lung cancer in Argentina in 2023 was estimated to be US$ 556.20 million (396.96 -718.20), approximately 1.4% of the total healthcare expenditure for the country. The cost increased with a higher stage of the disease and the main driver was the drug acquisition (80%). 179,046 Disability-adjusted life years could be attributable to lung cancer representing the 10% of the total cancer. Conclusion: The disease and economic burden of lung cancer in Argentina implies a high cost for the health system and would represent 19% of the previously estimated economic burden for 29 cancers in Argentina.

Title: Pan-tumor CAnine cuTaneous Cancer Histology (CATCH) dataset
Authors: Frauke Wilm, Marco Fragoso, Christian Marzahl, Jingna Qiu, Chloé Puget, Laura Diehl, Christof A. Bertram, Robert Klopfleisch, Andreas Maier, Katharina Breininger, Marc Aubreville
Date: Thu Jan 27 11:16:26 2022

Due to morphological similarities, the differentiation of histologic sections of cutaneous tumors into individual subtypes can be challenging. Recently, deep learning-based approaches have proven their potential for supporting pathologists in this regard. However, many of these supervised algorithms require a large amount of annotated data for robust development. We present a publicly available dataset of 350 whole slide images of seven different canine cutaneous tumors complemented by 12,424 polygon annotations for 13 histologic classes, including seven cutaneous tumor subtypes. In inter-rater experiments, we show a high consistency of the provided labels, especially for tumor annotations. We further validate the dataset by training a deep neural network for the task of tissue segmentation and tumor subtype classification. We achieve a class-averaged Jaccard coefficient of 0.7047, and 0.9044 for tumor in particular. For classification, we achieve a slide-level accuracy of 0.9857. Since canine cutaneous tumors possess various histologic homologies to human tumors the added value of this dataset is not limited to veterinary pathology but extends to more general fields of application.

Title: Learning Eligibility in Cancer Clinical Trials using Deep Neural Networks
Authors: Aurelia Bustos, Antonio Pertusa
Date: Thu Mar 22 11:38:53 2018

Interventional cancer clinical trials are generally too restrictive, and some patients are often excluded on the basis of comorbidity, past or concomitant treatments, or the fact that they are over a certain age. The efficacy and safety of new treatments for patients with these characteristics are, therefore, not defined. In this work, we built a model to automatically predict whether short clinical statements were considered inclusion or exclusion criteria. We used protocols from cancer clinical trials that were available in public registries from the last 18 years to train word-embeddings, and we constructed a~dataset of 6M short free-texts labeled as eligible or not eligible. A text classifier was trained using deep neural networks, with pre-trained word-embeddings as inputs, to predict whether or not short free-text statements describing clinical information were considered eligible. We additionally analyzed the semantic reasoning of the word-embedding representations obtained and were able to identify equivalent treatments for a type of tumor analogous with the drugs used to treat other tumors. We show that representation learning using {deep} neural networks can be successfully leveraged to extract the medical knowledge from clinical trial protocols for potentially assisting practitioners when prescribing treatments.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most frequent malignant disease in the world. In some countries with established screening programs, its incidence and mortality have decreased, and survival has improved. AIMS: To obtain reliable data about the epidemiology of CRC in Chile, we analyzed the trends in the last ten years and the influence of observable factors on survival, including explicit guarantees in CRC treatment access (GES program). Publicly available data published by the Health Ministry and National Institute of Statistics were used. Data were obtained from registries of mortality and hospital discharges, making follow-up of the individuals possible. Crude and age-standardized incidence and mortality rates were calculated, and individual survival was studied by constructing Kaplan-Meier curves. search_hits.retrieved_snippet:
【turn1044news21】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 2 months ago; Founders Fund, known for backing major tech companies like OpenAI and Airbnb, has invested $4 million in Gamgee, a veterinary biotech startup founded by Sydney engineer Paul Conyngham. Inspired by his determination to save his rescue dog Rosie from cancer using artificial intelligence, Conyngham developed a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine after chemotherapy failed. The treatment, supported by scientists at the University of NSW and the University of Queensland, extended Rosie's life by two years. Although Rosie was eventually euthanized due to an aggressive tumor recurrence, her legacy will continue through Gamgee’s upcoming clinical trials on 30–50 dogs with cancer. These trials aim to replicate Rosie's personalized vaccine treatment and will be free for pet owners. Influential figures such as OpenAI founder Sam Altman and Elon Musk have praised the initiative, with other notable seed investors joining the venture. Gamgee represents a promising intersection of AI and biotechnology, with aspirations to eventually extend its success to human treatments.
Founders Fund invests $4m in Gamgee, Rosie the dog’s AI cancer legacy
Date: Sun Aug 23 06:55:00 2026 UTC

The touching tale of puppy love convinced Founders Fund - which raised capital for OpenAI, Spotify, Facebook and Airbnb - to hand $4m in seed funding to Sydney engineer Paul Conyngham to set up a veterinary biotech company named Gamgee. The extraordinary investment - which followed Mr Conyngham's lunch with OpenAI founder Sam Altman - will allow Gamgee to conduct clinical trials on up to 50 more cancer-stricken canines in Australia this year. "I would never have believed in 1000 years that my little dog would have such a huge impact,'' he told The Australian from the US, where he has hired seven staff for his start-up. "It's been a wild ride to get this far. Founders Fund has backed some of the biggest companies on earth. I feel like this is a natural continuation of Rosie's legacy.'' How Sydney tech entrepreneur, Paul Conyngham, used artificial intelligence to create the world's first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, achieving remarkable tumour shrinkage that has astounded leading scientists. Founders Fund partner Amin Mirzadegan said he had been impressed by Mr Conyngham's "rare determination''. "What drew us to Paul was his love of Rosie - it led him to teach himself entirely new fields and push forward where most people would have stopped,'' the venture capitalist told The Australian. "That kind of determination is rare, and it's exactly what we look for in a founder. It also speaks to how AI is beginning to push the ball forward on science.'' Mr Conyngham's dogged use of artificial intelligence to devise an experimental cancer treatment for his pet dog Rosie convinced scientists from the University of NSW to help him sequence the DNA in Rosie's tumours to create a personalised mRNA vaccine to treat the dog's mast cell cancer, after chemotherapy had failed. University of Queensland veterinary researcher Professor Rachel Allavena then treated Rosie with the experimental vaccine, using pre-existing ethics approvals. Although the vaccine shrunk Rosie's tumours, she had to be ­euthanised in June at the age of nine, after one tumour grew back aggressively. "The AI extended her life by two years,'' Mr Conyngham said. "We had the cancer relatively contained until that point but something happened that caused the cancer to wake up and become extremely aggressive. "I don't know what happened, but the cancer came back very aggressively post-surgery - it was very sad to see.'' Mr Conyngham has named his start-up company Gamgee, after the Lord of the Rings character Samwise Gamgee - whose wife is named Rosie. He decided it was "an insanely cool name for this company''. So far he has hired seven staff - biologists, coders and marketers - to launch the new vet biotech company. Mr Conyngham said he was negotiating with University of Queensland to gain ethics and regulatory approval to replicate Rosie's treatment in a multi-site clinical trial involving between 30 and 50 dogs stricken with mast cell skin cancer or bone cancer, before the end of this year. He said he hoped to involve veterinarians along the eastern seaboard. Treatment, which would be free for owners, would involve taking a tissue sample from a dog's tumour, sequencing the DNA and then creating a customised immunotherapy treatment for injection back into the dog.

Queensland patient Mr. Pilkington, diagnosed in 2017 with aggressive prostate cancer, found new hope after nine years of extensive traditional therapies—including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, hormone, and immunotherapy—ceased to work. Since joining the trial in November 2025, he has experienced halted cancer progression and no side effects from the experimental drug, which significantly improved his quality of life. Professor Aaron Hansen, leading the trial through the Translational Research Institute, reported early success with the drug both in Australia and the US. The treatment has shown reduced tumour growth and fewer adverse effects compared to traditional methods. Encouraged by these outcomes, researchers are expanding the trial to recruit 20 additional participants nationwide. Meanwhile, rising prostate cancer rates among younger men underscore the urgency for new treatments. The Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia reports that incidence among men aged 30–49 has surged up to 500% since 2000, with related deaths in men under 50 increasing by 200% since 2014. For Mr. Pilkington, the clinical trial offers renewed hope and precious time with his family.

최근 만난 임성원(39) 임프리메드 대표는 지난 1년 간의 성과를 이렇게 말했다. 그는 미 실리콘밸리에서 바이오테크 스타트업 임프리메드를 이끈다. 인공지능 모델과 실험실 테스트를 통해 혈액암에 걸린 반려견을 대상으로 어떤 항암제가 효과적인지 예측하는 서비스를 제공한다.

이 업체는 작년부터 강아지를 넘어 사람 대상으로 서비스를 개발하고 있다. 본래 하려던 분야로, 최근 들어 성과가 나오고 있다. 임프리메드의 사람 대상 서비스가 완성되면 혈액암 환자들에게 어떤 치료법이 더 효과적인지 쉽게 알 수 있게 된다. 임 대표는 “우리의 목표는 시간이 생명인 암환자의 치료 과정에서 트라이-앤-에러(시행착오)를 줄이자는 것”이라고 했다.

### 临床招募｜犬三类肿瘤新药免费临床试验

2026-08-18

Image

家里狗狗确诊肥大细胞瘤、骨肉瘤、口腔鳞癌？

各位接诊此类病例的宠物医师请注意！

中农董军实验室抗肿瘤新药临床试验正式开启全国招募，符合条件的患病犬可免费使用抗肿瘤新药。

本次临床试验，既能大幅减轻宠物主人高额用药的经济压力，同时也会为犬类肿瘤治疗研发更安全有效的全新方案。

诚邀全国宠物医生积极推荐适配病例，也欢迎患病犬主咨询报名，推动小动物肿瘤诊疗水平持续提升。

* * *

三大实验组招募（名额有限）

试验组1：犬肥大细胞瘤

本次试验为新药初步临床效果研究，通过规范给药、定期复查监测，客观评估抗肿瘤药物对犬肥大细胞瘤的临床效果治疗新方案。

肿瘤状态：复发/未切除

试验组2：犬骨肉瘤

本次试验为新药初步临床效果研究，通过规范给药、定期复查监测，客观评估抗肿瘤药物对骨肉瘤的临床效果治疗新方案。

肿瘤状态：未截肢/肺部转移

试验组3：犬口腔鳞癌

本次试验为新药初步临床效果研究，通过规范给药、定期复查监测，客观评估抗肿瘤药物对口腔鳞癌的临床效果治疗新方案。

寵物產業因此衍生許多服務，例如寵物保險、寵物美容、寵物醫療、寵物國旅、寵物臨終送行，甚至寵物溝通等職業。而共信-KY鎖定伴侶動物疾病市場，針對犬類黑色素腫瘤部位注射治療，獲得初步臨床試驗成效，並於今(30)日正式提交農業部，申請寵物抗癌用藥。

市場法人表示，看好未來寵物癌症市場的潛力，共信-KY今年大舉招募寵物部門業務團隊，積極投入準備，加上剛於台灣動物醫院完成臨床試驗，與獸醫師們的互動良好，未來在靶向腫瘤消融新藥「思沛康注射液」成功上市銷售後，可望貢獻共信-KY營收成長動能。

資料顯示，過去十年來，癌症已躍升為老年犬貓十大死因第一名；然而，截至目前為止，在全球伴侶動物抗癌用藥市場上仍呈現相當大的市場需求，主要原因是目前對於伴侶動物罹患癌症的治療方式，仍是以手術搭配化療為主。公司指出，而這樣的標準治療對於動物傷害相當大，並已無法滿足因為少子化、老年化社會將犬貓視為家庭伴侶的關愛需求，共信-KY的PTS藥物具有靶向腫瘤消融特性，可望滿足此市場趨勢，商機潛力無窮。

The growing interest in human-grade total body positron emission tomography (PET) systems has also application in small animal research. In this work we present a novel system for generation of virtual PET images using CT scans. We combine a fully convolutional network (FCN) with a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) to generate simulated PET data from given input CT data. The synthesized PET can be used for false-positive reduction in lesion detection solutions. Clinically, such solutions may enable lesion detection and drug treatment evaluation in a CT-only environment, thus reducing the need for the more expensive and radioactive PET/CT scan. Title: Repositioning of 8565 existing drugs for COVID-19
Authors: Kaifu Gao, Duc Duy Nguyen, Jiahui Chen, Rui Wang, Guo-Wei Wei
Date: Wed May 20 13:20:52 2020

The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has infected near 5 million people and led to over 0.3 million deaths. Currently, there is no specific anti-SARS-CoV-2 medication. New drug discovery typically takes more than ten years. Drug repositioning becomes one of the most feasible approaches for combating COVID-19. This work curates the largest available experimental dataset for SARS-CoV-2 or SARS-CoV main protease inhibitors. Based on this dataset, we develop validated machine learning models with relatively low root mean square error to screen 1553 FDA-approved drugs as well as other 7012 investigational or off-market drugs in DrugBank. We found that many existing drugs might be potentially potent to SARS-CoV-2. The druggability of many potent SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitors is analyzed. This work offers a foundation for further experimental studies of COVID-19 drug repositioning.

Title: Text Classification of Cancer Clinical Trial Eligibility Criteria
Authors: Yumeng Yang, Soumya Jayaraj, Ethan B Ludmir, Kirk Roberts
Date: Thu Sep 14 15:59:16 2023

Automatic identification of clinical trials for which a patient is eligible is complicated by the fact that trial eligibility is stated in natural language. A potential solution to this problem is to employ text classification methods for common types of eligibility criteria. In this study, we focus on seven common exclusion criteria in cancer trials: prior malignancy, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, psychiatric illness, drug/substance abuse, and autoimmune illness. Our dataset consists of 764 phase III cancer trials with these exclusions annotated at the trial level. We experiment with common transformer models as well as a new pre-trained clinical trial BERT model. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of automatically classifying common exclusion criteria. Additionally, we demonstrate the value of a pre-trained language model specifically for clinical trials, which yields the highest average performance across all criteria.

Dairy farming plays an important role in agriculture for thousands of years not only in Sri Lanka but also in so many other countries. When it comes to dairy farming cattle is an indispensable animal. According to the literature surveys almost 3.9 million cattle and calves die in a year due to different types of diseases. The causes of diseases are mainly bacteria, parasites, fungi, chemical poisons and etc. Infectious diseases can be a greatest threat to livestock health. Human civilization is experiencing a critical situation that presents itself for a new coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). This virus emerged in late December 2019 in Wuhan city, Hubei, China. The grim fact of COVID-19 is, it is highly contagious in nature, therefore, spreads rapidly all over the world and causes severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Responding to the severity of COVID-19 research community directs the attention to the analysis of COVID-19, to diminish its antagonistic impact towards society. Numerous studies claim that the subcontinent, i.e., Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan, could remain in the worst affected region by the COVID-19. In order to prevent the spread of COVID-19, it is important to predict the trend of COVID-19 beforehand the planning of effective control strategies. Fundamentally, the idea is to dependably estimate the reproduction number to judge the spread rate of COVID-19 in a particular region. Consequently, this paper uses publicly available epidemiological data of Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan to estimate the reproduction numbers. More specifically, we use various models (for example, susceptible infection recovery (SIR), exponential growth (EG), sequential Bayesian (SB), maximum likelihood (ML) and time dependent (TD)) to estimate the reproduction numbers and observe the model fitness in the corresponding data set. Experimental results show that the reproduction numbers produced by these models are greater than 1.2 (approximately) indicates that COVID-19 is gradually spreading in the subcontinent.

This article summarizes the BCN20000 dataset, composed of 19424 dermoscopic images of skin lesions captured from 2010 to 2016 in the facilities of the Hospital Cl\'inic in Barcelona. With this dataset, we aim to study the problem of unconstrained classification of dermoscopic images of skin cancer, including lesions found in hard-to-diagnose locations (nails and mucosa), large lesions which do not fit in the aperture of the dermoscopy device, and hypo-pigmented lesions. Di tengah meningkatnya kasus limfoma pada anjing dan tantangan resistensi terhadap kemoterapi, salah satu dosen di Universitas Airlangga kembali menunjukkan kontribusinya dalam riset kanker hewan melalui sebuah studi kolaboratif dengan Yamaguchi University, Jepang. Penelitian ini mengungkap potensi besar obat target molekuler yaitu KPT‑335 (verdinexor), ketika dikombinasikan dengan kemoterapi konvensional dapat membuka peluang baru bagi terapi limfoma yang lebih efektif dan berkelanjutan.

Limfoma merupakan salah satu kanker hematopoietik paling umum pada anjing. Meskipun protokol CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) telah lama menjadi standar terapi, banyak pasien mengalami kekambuhan akibat resistensi obat. Kondisi ini tidak hanya menjadi tantangan klinis, tetapi juga beban emosional bagi pemilik hewan dan dokter hewan. KPT‑335 adalah inhibitor dari Exportin‑1 (XPO1), yaitu protein yang berperan mengangkut tumor suppressor keluar dari inti sel. Ketika XPO1 terlalu aktif, sel kanker dapat mematikan mekanisme pengawas internalnya. Dengan menghambat XPO1, KPT‑335 memungkinkan protein penekan tumor tetap berada di inti sel dan menjalankan fungsinya. Dalam penelitian ini, peneliti menemukan bahwa pengobatan dengan KPT-335 sebagai inhibitor XPO1 dapat mengurangi ekspresi protein XPO1 yang bergantung pada dosis secara signifikan, dan adanya penghambatan proteasome mampu membalikkan efek ini. Temuan ini mengonfirmasi bahwa obat tersebut tidak hanya menghambat fungsi XPO1, tetapi juga memicu degradasinya melalui jalur proteasomal.

Penelitian ini menguji kombinasi KPT‑335 dengan dua obat kemoterapi yang umum digunakan, yaitu doxorubicin dan vincristine. Empat garis sel limfoma anjing—dua tipe B dan dua tipe T—digunakan untuk mengevaluasi efektivitas kombinasi tersebut. Hasilnya menunjukkan bahwa kombinasi KPT‑335 dengan kedua kemoterapi tersebut menghasilkan penurunan proliferasi sel kanker yang jauh lebih besar dibandingkan penggunaan obat tunggal.
